episodes.165280: A line of strong to severe storms marched across Northern Alabama and Southern Middle Tennessee during the late afternoon hours and into the evening hours of the 22nd. As the evening progressed, the line of storms slowed down and caused more of a flooding threat. One tornado was reported in Northern Madison County, with several flooding reports from across the area.
episodes.165281: In addition to severe weather, excessive rainfall occurred causing numerous locations to experience flash flooding.  ||4-5.5 inches of rain in southern middle Tennessee.|20 roads closed due to flash flooding in Moore County alone.|Several roads closed in Lincoln County.|Schools closed on the 23rd as a result.
episodes.165715: A low pressure system tracking into the Great Lakes region swung a cold front into the Ohio Valley on February 22nd. Rain showers increased that evening as the surface front scooted closer towards southeast Ohio. The river gages for the Muskingum River at Beverly and McConnelsville as well as the gage for Duck Creek at Macksburg noted a rise due to the influx of rainfall, which resulted in minor flooding while the river and creek were out of their banks.
episodes.166161: An area of low pressure moved across the region bringing mild and windy weather along with periods of rainfall, some heavy enough, to cause localized areas of flooding. An ice jam also developed in the Village of Dolgeville leading to flooding along the East Canada Creek.
episodes.166306: A stalled cold front moved into northwest Georgia late on February 22, 2022. This front combined with anomalously moist and unstable conditions to produce training showers and thunderstorms that resulted in heavy rainfall over northwest Georgia. A Flood Watch was issued for north Georgia, and while widespread flash flooding was not observed, isolated river flooding occurred in Dade and Catoosa counties. The rapid rise of Lookout Creek in Dade County occurred in under 6 hours.
episodes.166782: A line of thunderstorms ahead of a slow moving cold front produced periods of heavy rainfall over a several period over the northwest portions of central Alabama.  Rainfall totals averaged 2-3 inches.
episodes.166886: A moist southwesterly flow aloft ran nearly parallel to a stalled cold front near east Tennessee on the 23rd. A surface low near Lake Charles LA would move up the boundary and produce a second round of rains on the 24th.
episodes.166947: On February 17 and 18th a strong low pressure system tracked through southern Canada and ushered in an unseasonably warm and moist airmass. Temperatures surged into the 50s to low 60s. Steady rainfall accompanied by embedded heavier showers with the cold frontal passage produced about 0.75 inches of precipitation. Wind, high humidity, and rain resulted in significant snowmelt where snow was ripe. Runoff was sufficient to raise area rivers, though most remained in their banks. River rises resulted in ice breakup and minor ice jam flooding on some rivers across central New Hampshire, which continued for several days.  The largest impacts were reported in the Claremont region.
episodes.166949: Numerous thunderstorms developed across northeast Mississippi in the warm and unstable airmass ahead of an approaching cold front. A storm became severe in Monroe County with damaging wind.
episodes.167085: Numerous showers and thunderstorms affected Middle Tennessee on February 22. Some of the storms became severe with a few reports of large hail and wind damage. In addition, heavy rainfall resulted in flooding across several areas of Middle Tennessee. Rainfall totals from February 21 to February 25 ranged from 3 to over 7 inches fell across the area, which led to widespread river flooding on most rivers and streams across the region through the rest of the month.

events.narrative: Three power poles were broken on Strong Road.

The Muskingum River in McConnelsville rose out of its 11 foot flood stage on the evening of February 22nd. Just after midnight on the 23rd, the river crested at 11.59 feet and returned to its banks just before noon that morning. Several roads observed high water spilling from the river, including Route 669 near Malta and down into McConnelsville. Several homes near the river also observed minor flooding.

The main damage indicators from this tornado were at least 2 downed or uprooted trees and multiple areas of large branches that were downed by the winds. The damage occurred mainly along Grimwood Drive, west of U.S. Highway 431 in Hazel Green. Damage also extended into a neighborhood off Grimwood Drive near Bentley and Cherrywood Drive. Very minor, small branch damage was noted just east of U.S. Highway 431 on Walker Lane south of Briar Crest Rd. This is likely where the weak, short-lived tornado dissipated.

In the town of Beverly, the Muskingum River rose out of its 29 foot flood stage late in the evening of February 22nd, cresting at 30.72 feet during the predawn hours of the 26th, and returning to its banks later that evening. Floodwaters spilled onto the nearby fields and farmlands while the river was out of its banks.

In Macksburg, Duck Creek rose above its 13 foot bankfull level just after midnight on February 23rd. The creek crested at 13.44 feet around noon that day and returned to its banks a few hours later. While the creek was out of its banks, minor flooding occurred in fields and campgrounds within close vicinity of the gage.

Runoff from heavy rainfall over the area produced a rise on Lookout Creek near New England (USGS 03568933 / NWS ENGG1). The river rose above Minor Flood stage at 330 AM and crest at 15.71 ft at 1030 AM before beginning to fall. Radar estimates indicate that between 2 and 4 inches of rain occurred quickly over the area, and the rapid rise of the creek occurred in under 6 hours.
